title: Even a gnat
hookLine: Allah is not shy to strike a parable of a gnat (2:26)
carry: nothing is too small to teach

lines: A FLY? A SPIDER? FROM GOD?
cards: It's summer, it's late, and something tiny is whining near your ear. You slap at it in the dark and miss. A creature the size of an eyelash has just taken over your whole night.
Small things are like that: easy to dismiss, right up until they aren't. Some early listeners, the commentators report, dismissed the Qur'an for talking about small things at all.
A book from God, they said, mentioning flies and spiders? Al-Baqarah answers them. Today: even a gnat.

teach.b: The Qur'an uses small creatures as teachers. Elsewhere it says the idols people call on couldn't create a single fly, and couldn't even take back what a fly steals from them.

It compares a flimsy refuge to a spider's house, the frailest of houses. The commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, report that some listeners scoffed at this, and that verse twenty-six of al-Baqarah answers them.
In Pickthall's words: “Lo! Allah disdaineth not to coin the similitude even of a gnat.” The Arabic word is ba'udah, a gnat or a mosquito.

teach.h: NOT TOO PROUD FOR A GNAT
teach.b: The literal sense of the verb is closer to: God is not shy, not too proud, to strike a likeness of a gnat, or of what is above it. That little phrase, what is above it, split the commentators.
Some said it means anything bigger than a gnat. Others said it means beyond it in smallness: whatever is even tinier. Either way, size doesn't decide what can teach.
The verse goes on to say that the same parable leads some people astray and guides others.

teach.h: THE GNAT STAYS; THE LISTENER CHANGES
teach.b: The gnat doesn't change. The listener does. One person hears a mosquito and rolls their eyes.
Another sees in it something made with care, a body, wings, a will to live, balanced in a frame you can barely see. Whole surahs carry the names of small creatures: the bee, the ant, the spider.

how: Muslims point to the Qur'an's many parables from nature, and to surahs named for the bee, the ant and the spider, as invitations to reflect on small created things as signs.

o: a bee, which has a surah named for it
a gnat or mosquito, small enough to miss
a spider, whose house is the frailest

s: the Qur'an avoids mentioning small creatures
it speaks of the fly, the spider, the gnat, and names surahs for the bee and the ant.
commentators disagree whether what is above it means bigger or smaller
some say anything bigger; others say beyond it in smallness.
the verse says the same parable guides some and misleads others
the gnat doesn't change; the listener does.

games.q: listeners mock: why would God talk about flies and spiders? how does al-Baqarah answer?
o: God is not too proud to strike a likeness of even a gnat.
games.why: it doubles down: God disdains not the likeness of even a gnat. the size of the teacher was never the point.

practice: Look closely at something tiny: a crumb, a seed, an ant on the windowsill, the grain of the wood on your table, a single letter on this screen.
Bring your eyes close and look longer than feels normal, at its edges, its color, any movement. Then close your eyes, breathe, and ask quietly what it could teach if it were a parable.

wordCard.voice: Ba'udah. A gnat or mosquito — the small creature al-Baqarah says God is not too proud to use as a likeness. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a gnat or a mosquito, the creature in 2:26.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing is too small to teach. A gnat can be a teacher too. Day three hundred thirty-eight, done.

sources.q: Lo! Allah disdaineth not to coin the similitude even of a gnat.
